data.title: Trump urges GOP to keep Senate in session until college sports bill passes
data.description:
President Trump on Friday ramped up the pressure on Senate Republicans to cancel part of their August recess, this time urging embattled GOP senators to stay in Washington until they pass a bill to reform rules for compensating and recruiting college athletes.

The measure has been bogged down in the Senate, and the disagreement over the measure appears to be holding up a deal to speedily advance other priorities.

“THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT is a great Bill, and the Senate will hopefully stay in D.C. until it passes,” Trump declared on Truth Social.

“Without this Bill, millions of young Athletes will be hurt, programs will be canceled, Women’s and Olympic Sports will go away, the fans will be robbed, and Universities will go broke,” Trump warned.

The Senate Republican cloakroom on Friday circulated a “hotline” alert to gauge potential objections to the college sports bill, a bipartisan measure that was negotiated by Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

The measure would establish nationwide standards for name, image and likeness (NIL), transfers and eligibility for college sports.

Cruz is pushing for unanimous consent to vote on the bill before the Senate leaves for a five-week recess.

The “hotline” circulated by Senate GOP leaders proposed voting on a motion to proceed to the bill and, if it’s successful, a follow-up vote to pass the legislation at a 60-vote threshold.

But one senior Senate GOP aide said there are multiple objections to advancing the bill so quickly.

“It’s complicated, there are a lot of pieces to this. I’m okay with waiting,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), whose home state includes the SEC powerhouse the University of Georgia.

The Aflac Kickoff Game last month offered a major name, image and likeness deal with Auburn leading up to its game against Baylor on Sept. 5.

The SEC and Big Ten conferences initially opposed the Protect College Sports Act but recently issued a statement expressing support for the legislation after negotiating changes with the bill’s authors.

Some Republicans, including Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), have expressed concern the legislation as drafted could overturn laws passed in 27 states barring transgender athletes from women’s sports.

Trump on Friday insisted the bill would not override those state laws.

“Nobody has done more to protect Women Athletes than me — and this Bill CLEARLY protects the Laws in 27 States protecting Women’s Sports, and banning Men from Women’s Sports. Anyone who tells you differently is LYING! Stop grandstanding, and try getting this done,” Trump declared on Truth Social.

Trump had previously demanded that the Senate cancel its August recess to continue debating and voting on the SAVE America Act, which would require people to prove citizenship when registering to vote and require voters show photo identification in federal elections.

The president has also urged the Senate not to leave for the August recess before passing a budget resolution to set the state for passing a third reconciliation package to provide new funding for the Pentagon, struggling farmers and grants to states to adopt election reforms.

Thune has proposed voting on a motion to proceed to the budget resolution before senators leave town for the recess.

data.title: Alito to WSJ: 'Obviously I'm here for another term'
data.description:
Justice Samuel Alito shut down any notion he’s planning to imminently retire from the Supreme Court in an interview with The Wall Street Journal published Friday. 

It marks the justice’s first known comments on his future plans since NPR erroneously reported that the conservative jurist had announced his retirement on the final opinion day of the court’s term. 

“Obviously I’m here for another term,” Alito told the Journal’s opinion section. 

Alito has never publicly suggested he intends to retire, but NPR’s report came amid speculation that he may step aside so President Trump could nominate a replacement while Republicans hold a majority in the Senate. 

At 76, Alito is the court’s second-oldest justice, behind Justice Clarence Thomas, 78. But both are still younger than the most recent justices who’ve retired. 

Alito’s interview lands as the justice gears up to publish his first, full-length book in October as the court kicks off its next term. 

“It’s not pleasant, in the sense that it’s a reminder of mortality,” Alito said in the interview, in reference to the retirement rumors. “It’s like, what are those vultures doing up there? They are flying around. But it goes with life tenure.” 

The justice also pushed back on critics who’ve taken aim at him for dissenting in favor of Trump in recent major decisions on tariffs, birthright citizenship and the firing of a Federal Reserve governor. 

“I vote in every case the way I think the case should be decided. If that means a high correlation with what Trump wants, fine. If it means zero correlation with what Trump wants, fine as well,” Alito told the Journal. 

The justice said he wouldn’t decide a cases the other way simply so people would call him objective. He called that “absolutely wrong.” 

“There have been people who’ve recommended to me that I do that. I’m not going to do that,” he said in the interview.

data.title: Trump restarts effort to fire Fed's Lisa Cook: Reports
data.description:
President Trump is reportedly renewing his effort to boot Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook from her position, despite the Supreme Court thwarting his earlier attempt in June.

A letter from White House presidential aide Dan Scavino, dated Wednesday, said the president was “considering” removing her, according to a copy of the letter obtained by PBS NewsHour.

The letter was first reported by ABC News.

It said there was “sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements.”

It also asked her to “prove a written response with your explanation for your false statements and accompanying evidence,” within three weeks.

Trump first tried to fire Cook last August over accusations of mortgage fraud in an unprecedented move. It came after a referral from Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, who suggested Cook illegally designated properties she had in Michigan and Georgia as primary residences to receive better financing terms.

She fought the firing and pushed back on the allegations, arguing that it was spurred by Trump’s frustrations over the central bank not lowering the interest rates quickly enough.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that she can remain on the job as the case moves forward.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote at the time that Trump didn’t give Cook due process to contest the allegations, but also noted that whether she can removed “for cause will depend in part on the underlying facts.”

“In this opinion, we have not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards. Rather, we have simply addressed the parties’ arguments about the appropriate legal standards under which the facts must be evaluated,” he wrote.

In a statement, Cook’s legal team said they will fight “this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed.”

“These allegations are as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve,” the statement said. “No matter was President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent – there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. The Federal Reserve declined to comment.

data.title: Spokesman for Chuck Edwards blasts Ethics panel, report: 'Not driven by due process'
data.description:
Rep. Chuck Edwards’s (R-N.C.) spokesman Paul Shumaker slammed the House Ethics Committee panel that cited him for inappropriate behavior following Edwards dropping his reelection bid for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. 

In an appearance on PBS’s “State Lines,” Shumaker called out his issues with the House Ethics report that resulted in Edwards’s drop from the election.

“First of all, there was never a forward complaint lodged against Congressman Edwards. It was taken off. The committee chose to do the work based upon anonymous news sources and news stories that had been generated,” Shumaker said.

The report on Edwards, released Monday, recommended he be formally censured by the full House because he had violated “the spirit” of the chamber’s rules against sexual harassment and unwanted advances.

The Ethics Committee continued in the report that Edwards’s behavior with “two young staffers, repeatedly over a sustained period, was beyond inappropriate.”

Shumaker disagreed with this assessment and stated the committee gave “less than an adequate amount of time” to Edwards’s legal team to respond to the allegations.

Edwards’s attorney did formally respond over the weekend to the report, saying the recommendation for censure was based on “vague standards requiring credible behavior and adherence to the spirit of the Rules of the House” rather than rules violating sexual misconduct.

“The committee had already been in the field, polling on this issue and looking for other alternatives. So, you have a process that’s driven totally by politics, not driven by due process,” Shumaker added.

Shumaker confirmed that Republican leadership had asked Edwards to step down by Tuesday following the allegations. Edwards announced early Wednesday on social platform X he would drop his reelection bid but would complete his current term in the House.

“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” he wrote.

North Carolina Republicans have not announced his replacement that will appear on ballots in the general election.

data.title: Murkowski, Merkley demand answers on Trump's Smithsonian disclaimers
data.description:
A bipartisan pair of lawmakers are requesting more information from the Trump administration about its plans to install disclaimers outside of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (NMAH). 

GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley (Ore.) — the chair and ranking member on the Senate Interior Appropriations Subcommittee — expressed concern about this project in a Thursday letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. 

Executive Order 14416, “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution,” compels Burgum, alongside National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron and the assistant to the president for domestic policy, to install temporary signage outside of this museum to warn visitors about alleged inaccuracies included in its exhibits. 

“For the past 180 years, the Smithsonian Institution has been committed to sharing objective historical evidence through research and education, not political narratives,” the lawmakers wrote. 

“The Smithsonian Institution has worked tirelessly to present a comprehensive narrative of our nation’s amazing history, from its many triumphs to its trials,” they continued. “There is nothing more American than telling our story truthfully.”

This signage installation project is the latest in President Trump’s and his administration’s efforts to crack down on the Smithsonian Institute over exhibits they say do not align with their view of American history. 

In his executive order last month, the president cited the results of a report produced by the White House Domestic Policy Council, which conducted a months-long review of the NMAH’s exhibits. 

“The Report demonstrates that the Smithsonian leadership does not present American history as a shared national inheritance to be taught and celebrated, but instead views American history as a ‘prime tool’ to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society,” the president said in his executive order.  

The Smithsonian Institute declined to comment at the time this order was issued. 

Murkowski and Merkley requested that the Interior secretary provide Congress with more information about these disclaimers, including the cost of their installation, a map displaying the signs’ locations and quantity and the length of their “temporary” installation. 

The Hill has reached out to the Interior Department for comment.

data.title: Judge rejects SPLC bid to dismiss case as 'vindictive' prosecution
data.description:
A federal judge in Alabama denied the Southern Poverty Law Center’s (SPLC) bid to dismiss a case brought by the Trump administration on the grounds it amounted to a vindictive prosecution, finding the civil rights nonprofit did not meet the bar to demonstrate the Justice Department was motivated by animus in bringing the case.

Throughout the order, U.S. District Judge Emily Marks blasted both parties in the case for “heated rhetoric, better suited for cable news, or a podcast.”

But she said SPLC failed to meet the requirements for the court to grant further discovery on their claims of vindictiveness, let alone dismiss the case in its entirely.

“Federal courts are not the proper forum for airing political grievances. For that reason, the doctrine of vindictive prosecution places a heavy burden on the accused, and decades of precedent counsels against its application here. Two things can be true at once: critics are not constitutionally immunized solely because they speak frequently and prosecutorial decisions may be second guessed—if they evince some evidence of animus,” Marks, a Trump appointee, wrote in the order.

“Missing here is the requisite objective evidence to show that the United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Alabama (on its own accord or at the direction of others) prosecuted the SPLC for exercising its First Amendment rights.”

The Trump administration has alleged that the SPLC defrauded donors by working with embeds who were spying on various white supremacist and extremist groups. Their indictment alleges that by paying these informants, the SPLC was funding the very groups it claimed to be fighting.

It’s a claim the SPLC strongly denies — one it says is “not even supported by or contained in the indictment itself.” It also has accused prosecutors of misleading the grand jury to gain an indictment.

The SPLC has vehemently denied any wrongdoing, including taking any actions that would undermine its effort to fight hate groups. It has said its donors were well aware they were spying on extremists.

“While the Southern Poverty Law Center is disappointed with the outcome of the motion, we will continue to vigorously defend ourselves, our staff and our work,” an SPLC spokesperson said Friday.

“SPLC will continue to fight hate, and we will continue to envision and create a safer and more just world. The actions by the DOJ will not shake our resolve to fight for justice and ensure the promise of the Civil Rights movement becomes a reality for all.”

Tensions between the SPLC and some conservatives have been building for years, particularly through the group’s “Hate Map” and other work documenting the ideologies of various groups. That includes some that have been supportive of Trump, such as Charlie Kirk’s Turning Point USA and the Proud Boys. 

The SPLC argues Turning Point belonged on its list because Kirk had “warned his hundreds of thousands of listeners” they were being replaced by foreigners.

Shortly after Kirk’s death, the FBI cut ties with the group, severing a relationship in which the nonprofit passed along intelligence it gained from spying on extremists.

“The Southern Poverty Law Center long ago abandoned civil rights work and turned into a partisan smear machine. Their so-called ‘hate map’ has been used to defame mainstream Americans and even inspired violence. That disgraceful record makes them unfit for any FBI partnership,” FBI Director Kash Patel wrote at the time.

data.title: Hillary Clinton calls for unity within Democratic Party: 'It can't be a one-way street'
data.description:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton urged Democrats on Friday to unify under its candidates, highlighting the growing division between establishment and progressive party leaders amid the current wave of primaries.

Clinton told journalist and podcaster Kara Swisher that, with Democratic candidates like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed winning their races by slim margins, the party should prepare for voters’ “reluctance” — which she said she experienced first-hand after being chosen as Democrats’ presidential nominee in 2016.

In mid-July, Democratic strategist James Carville called the new wave of progressives “insurgent” following recent wins from democratic socialists and similarly warned against inner-party division. This past Tuesday, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Carville to “start his own party” as the pundit continued his criticism of Democratic candidates.

“I think there’s no doubt that the Republican Party is the Trump Cult and the Democratic Party is a bigger tent,” Clinton told Swisher. “We do have a broad cross-section of people, what they believe, what their experiences are. I think that’s an advantage, but we also have to win general elections.”

The former secretary of state focused El-Sayed’s narrow victory over left-leaning moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Wednesday in the race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.). He will face the Trump-endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in this fall’s midterms.

One of the policy areas where El-Sayed and his challenger differed was their stances on United States aid to Israel — a point of contention that resonates throughout the Democratic Party.

The Michigan candidate for Senate, like some other progressive Democrats, called Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide.” He also criticized the Stevens campaign’s ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), a group that has grown increasingly controversial among party members.

“The real fight will be how do we make sure that people who voted for Haley feel comfortable voting for Abdul El-Sayed, and how do we get Independents to feel comfortable,” Clinton said.

In her appearance, the former secretary of state also referenced President Trump’s several Truth Social posts calling El-Sayed a communist, one of which referred to the Democratic nominee as a “Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel” and called his victory “great news for the Republican Party.”

Republicans have similarly targeted Democratic Socialists of America candidates, who also saw a series of primary wins, with the “communist” label. Clinton said she anticipates this framing of progressive Democrat and DSA candidates will be “very effective” for Republicans.

El-Sayed, whom Trump criticized throughout a Las Vegas speech earlier this week, responded to the president’s remarks in an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins Wednesday evening, inviting him to “focus on what I’m saying” regarding policy.

data.title: Trump announces deals and investments to bolster mining
data.description:
President Trump on Friday announced a slate of deals and investments that aim to bolster mining, something the administration has said will boost the economy and secure supply chains.

Trump said during a mining roundtable that the Defense Department would sign a $1.4 billion loan agreement with Sila nanotechnologies to build a battery facility in Washington state. The department is also investing $400 million to advance production of scandium, which Trump described as an aerospace and defense material, in Australia and another $150 million in a rare earth magnet facility in Minnesota.

He also said the U.S. Export-Import bank is “working to provide” more than $1 billion to finance Ivanhoe Electric’s copper mine in Arizona and would also seek to support an Alabama graphite project and a California Boron facility. 

He also said that the administration would be doling out $100 million for mining schools to “train the next generation of American miners.”

“Together we’re reawakening the spirit of the Gold Rush,” Trump said. “Very simply, we’re making mining great again.”

The push for more U.S. minerals comes as China has significant control over much of the world’s supply chains as a major miner, refiner and trader of these materials. 

Minerals are used in a range of technologies including weapons, semiconductors and renewable energy.

data.title: Live updates: Senate searches for path to finish to-do list; Cassidy will back Blanche's nomination
data.description:
The Senate is searching for a path to wrap up its to-do list and leave for a month-long recess, but a bipartisan bill to set rules for compensating and recruiting college athletes is holding up a broader deal.

The chamber is trying to find an agreement on quickly passing its top priorities before leaving: a stopgap government funding bill and confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general. The so-called NIL bill, however, has become a “chokepoint,” one senator reportedly said.

The stopgap funding bill has found overwhelming bipartisan support on earlier procedural votes.

And Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said Friday morning in a Senate floor speech that he will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, likely allowing his nomination to pass the Senate. Cassidy was the final holdout on the nomination.

As the lame duck senator announced his decision, he hesitated, noting he would catch criticism for his decision but assuring his Louisiana constituents that he had thoughtfully considered the vote.

The Senate earlier Friday overwhelmingly passed a bill that will allow for new sanctions on Russia. The legislation, named for its champion, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), passed 86-11.

President Trump on Friday has policy meetings at the White House and a roundtable at the State Department, before heading to Bedminster, N.J.

Follow live here.

data.title: Ex-Trump aide: Vance is 'negative rizz'
data.description:
Former deputy press secretary Sarah Matthews said Vice President Vance does not have the charisma that President Trump has following an incident where Vance fat-shamed a conservative pundit.

Matthews, in an appearance on CNN’s “NewsNight” on Friday, discussed a post on the social platform X from Vance that weighed in on an ongoing debate about burrito affordability.

During the segment, Matthews said, “People are receptive to Trump’s trolling, but I don’t think people are as receptive to JD Vance’s because Trump is at least, like him or not, charismatic. JD Vance is negative rizz when it comes to charisma.”

“I’m surprised to hear Mark say this. If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito,” Vance wrote in the post responding to Washington Post columnist Marc Thiessen.

When asked about the tweet on the Hugh Hewitt’s Salem News Channel show on Thursday, Vance said the post was a joke.

“Maybe in two years you’ll look back and say, ‘I wish I hadn’t said that’ but right now I feel pretty good about that,” Vance said.

Vance is currently being evaluated by the Republican party for a potential 2028 presidential run alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

President Trump pushed back on a report that said he pushed donors to back Vance in 2028, stating to reporters, “I think he’s great, but we’re way too early to even be thinking about that.”

The competition between Vance and Rubio has largely remained behind closed doors with the vice president likening it to the Trump’s former reality show, “The Apprentice.”

“I just don’t think it sounds like the president of the United States to have a televised competition for who would succeed him as his apprentice,” Vance said at a press conference in May. “I just think that’s not at all what you would expect the president to do.”

A straw poll from last week done in the Western Conservative Summit found that 57 percent of the 500-plus respondents backed Rubio, with Vance coming in second at 21 percent.
